 Associated Press 
 TODAY'S GAME
 Teams: No. 21 Iowa (6-2, 2-2) at Northwestern (6-2, 3-2)
 Where: Ryan Field, Evanston, Ill.
 Kickoff: 6:30 p.m.
 TV: KFXA
 Odds: Northwestern by 2.5
 IOWA CITY — No. 19 Iowa football’s north end zone of Kinnick Stadium has been known to cause some chaos for opponents. It stands over 100 feet tall, and it has helped Iowa use its fanbase to help force false starts, among other things.
 Iowa fans remember the three-straight false starts against Penn State in 2021, and the many other times back-to-back false starts or delay-of-game penalties caused frustration for Big Ten foes or other nonconference teams.
 Only Iowa’s defense knows what the north end zone is truly like. The offense is getting a glimpse of that experience Saturday night.
 Northwestern just introduced something very similar to the north end zone in its new Ryan Field: the Wildcat Wall. It’s a European-football style stadium with a 65-percent slope, according to Northwestern’s website, and is filled with 2,000 students all standing on top of the end zone.
 “I'm excited to play there, but they do have that student section wall or something, apparently,” offensive lineman Trevor Lauck said. “So it could get loud. But we’re going to have to go on a silent cadence.”
 Iowa offensive lineman Trevor Lauck (59) lines up for action against Washington during a Big Ten Conference football game Oct. 9 in Seattle.
 Associated Press 
 The new Ryan Field won’t be the largest stadium Iowa’s been to this season — that’ll be Michigan Stadium back in Week 4. But it’s a new experience for the Hawkeyes, something that head coach Kirk Ferentz hasn’t dealt with before.
 “It looks like a beautiful facility. It has to be great for everybody there. I just know what moving into this facility did for us and then even the Pacha North End Zone project was really uplifting,” Ferentz said Tuesday. “We're prepared for everything. In this conference you have to be. We'll always work on the silent cadence any time we're on the road, but yeah, anxious to find out. More anxious to see how we play, because that's going to be the challenge.”
 Quarterback Hank Brown and the offensive line have typically used a silent cadence on road games, so that element of the game hasn’t change. Brown’s performance against Wisconsin a week ago, earning himself the first Big Ten Offensive Player of the Week nod for an Iowa quarterback since 2018, helps give the starting QB some extra confidence heading into another hostile environment.
 Even with the player of the week worthy performance, Brown said he knows what he’ll need to improve on before heading up to the Chicago area against a Wildcat defense looking for a bounce-back win over their own following a loss at Oregon.
 “They play super hard,” Brown said. “They’re very fundamentally sound. It’ll obviously be a good matchup, and I’m super, super excited to play in this new stadium.”
 Iowa’s offensive line will also feature Michael Myslinski at center this week, Ferentz said, with Cael Winter out this week. The Hawkeyes have caught themselves with pre-snap penalties a handful of times this year — and this week’s not one to let those add up.
 Clear communication, even with the silent cadence, will help the Hawkeyes find success.
 And it’ll help turn the ruckus of the Wildcat Wall into a silent wall of Northwestern fans.
 “We'll switch up obviously as the game's going on. But we’re prepared to go on a silent cadence,” Lauck said. “That kind of — I wouldn't say is a challenge, but something definitely — we’d rather be playing at home, for sure.”
